customize.text: Adepti

Adepti are immortal illuminated beasts of Liyue, who have protected people for millennia. As humans have a higher purpose, only those of non-human status can be Adepti. No one is born an Adeptus, and no one remains an Adeptus forever, so all of non-human status can become an Adeptus. The word "Adeptus" is merely a title, so not all illuminated beasts are referred to as such. The Adepti are known as the "mighty and illuminated" Adepti, and this "illumination" refers to the light of a third "eye" that they possess, which allows them to use elemental powers without a Vision. For humans, the third "eye" takes the form of a Vision, but Adepti, pure elemental beings, are closer to the origin of ultimate truth than ordinary mortals. They were born amongst the elemental energy that courses between heaven and earth, so channeling elemental power is something that can be done almost subconsciously. They do not require the aid of an external focus to do so, let alone a Vision. It is not known for certain how Adepti get their Visions, however, when they take the human form, they tend to use a Vision to follow human rules.

Half-Adepti, who have a mixture of human and illuminated beast blood flowing through their veins, likely can't change their form and have an appearance of both illuminated beasts and humans/ Thus, Ganyu has horns, and Yanfei has antlers and scales. Their life expectancy is much longer than ordinary people because some half-Adepti live for more than 3,000 years. Although half-Adepti have a natural ability to resonate with the world, they receive Visions like mortal people, which help them to enhance their powers.

Rex Lapis, the Geo Archon, is the Prime of Adepti who can bless other Adepti as part of their "illumination." One such blessing is the ability to create small, autonomous pocket worlds and Adepti's abodes. Although Adepti of the north, Fujin and Herblord, were worshiped as Adepti, they don't have an Adeptal name and don't have some of the southern Adepti powers, like the ability to create abodes. Each Adeptus has their own powers. Thus, Rex Lapis and Menogias could control the Geo element, Xiao and Cloud Retainer could control the Anemo element, Indarias could control Pyro, and Bonanus and Bosacius could control Hydro and Electro powers, respectively. Adepti can use their powers even to save humans from death, although mortals can't bear such energy.
When Adepti die, there's a tradition of "sending Adepti off," which is called the Rite of Parting and allows Adepti to ascend. This Rite is a ceremony that requires special costumes, a special time, place, weather, and an audience. Some people believe that Adepti ascended to Celestia or were even born there, but no one really knows the truth of their birth and death.

Many Adepti live in Jueyun Karst, which is considered the realm of the Adepti of Liyue, usually unreachable by mortals. However, there are special "Herb Gatherers" who make their living by collecting valuable natural resources found only in Jueyun Karst. Other mortals need the special Sigil of Permission to enter the sacred lands. Some Adepti make traps for careless travelers and Treasure Hoarders, so no one will disturb them.

customize.text: Archon War

Long before the Archon War, when Rex Lapis had not yet received a Gnosis, he, along with other Gods and Adepti, founded Liyue and the Guili Assembly. Guizhong, the God of Dust, imparted her wisdom along with her skill to craft machinery onto humanity. Marchosius, the Stove God, gave people the knowledge of cooking and creating ovens. Together with other Adepti, they defended their people. In those distant times, Adepti of the south, who served Rex Lapis, were friends with Adepti of the north, who served another Goddess. Adepti often had tea parties, spent their time together, played music, and sang.

When the Archon War began, Liyue's lands became a battlefield. The Goddess of the north and her servants, Fujin and Herblord, fought with Rex Lapis; the Guili Plains were flooded, and the Adepti helped the inhabitants to move to Liyue Harbor, which later became the main city. Many Adepti were killed in this war. Marchosius sacrificed himself for the people, losing his powers and memory and turning into Guoba. Skybracer sacrificed his antlers to support a collapsing mountain, ensuring the safety of villagers, and kept on fighting until his blood was drained and his life ran out. Herblord and Fujin went against their Goddess to protect people and lost all their Adeptal energy. 3700 years ago, Adepti entered into a contract with Rex Lapis and promised to protect Liyue Harbor.

After the Archon War, the lands of Liyue were plagued by pestilence and famine. The rotting remains of the defeated gods spread across the world, reborn into demons. The monsters' rage manifested in the form of diseases, monster infestations, and other strange occurrences. Then, Rex Lapis summoned the Yakshas to vanquish the demons. They swore an oath: <color=#ffffffd9>"Restore order through slaughter, purge evil through battle. To this, we dedicate our lives."</color> Being the most fierce and warlike of all the Adepti, they were ready to do anything to protect the lands.

Long ago, during the war between the Adepti and demons, a girl named Qiqi wandered into the realm of the Adepti. While out gathering herbs, she injured her right leg in a fall and sought refuge in a cavern. As she was bandaging her leg, Qiqi could hear the sounds of battle in the distance. Caught in the crossfire, during the final moments of her life, Qiqi feared death. Longing to live and missing her family, Qiqi yearned to return to the happier days. She reflected, if only she could freeze time, and tears fell from her moribund eyes upon the Vision that had appeared before her. Perhaps it was this girl's pure desire to live that ended the war between the Adepti and demons, as the heavens willed. The Adepti could not bear to let her die, and each imparted a portion of their strength to her, meaning to breathe life back into her body. Qiqi was revived, but the unbridled power of the Adepti seething within her soon drove her insane. Seeking to end the disturbance, Mountain Shaper had no choice but to seal the hapless maiden in amber. Hundreds of years later, the amber containing Qiqi was discovered by mortals and later given to the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor for burial. During transportation along a bumpy road, Qiqi awakened, broke the amber, and escaped. Following her old habit of gathering herbs, she headed into the mountain forest to resume her task, and it was there that she met Doctor Baizhu. The owner of the Bubu Pharmacy, obsessed with achieving eternal life, agreed to take Qiqi in as his apprentice.

customize.text: Death of Rex Lapis

After defeating all the rival gods in Liyue during the Archon War,
ascended to the divine throne to receive the Geo Gnosis and become the Geo Archon. Together with the Adepti, Morax ruled the Nation of Contracts, and soon Liyue became a major trading nation. 3,700 years into his reign, Morax decided to pass the rule of Liyue to the Adepti and its people, ultimately leaving the post of an Archon. To achieve this goal, he played out his death in front of the mortals of the region and entered into "a contract to end all contracts" with the Cryo Archon. While the loss of his divine ability to defend Liyue was too great a price to pay, the Tsaritsa was able to offer Morax a deal that balanced the scales, and in exchange, Rex Lapis gave his Gnosis to the Fatui Harbinger, Signora.

During the performance, Morax orchestrated his own death at one of the Rites of Descension. Upon learning of the incident, the Adepti were furious, believing that the Qixing, Liyue's mortal rulers, had failed in their duties by allowing for the Archon's death. Cloud Retainer sought to annihilate all of Liyue Harbor, convinced that the Archon's death would herald catastrophic events. She believed that the people needed to be liberated from the impending turmoil that would ensue. Once Rex Lapis came to them in a dream, the Adepti decided to temporarily reconcile with Liyue Qixing to protect people from the threat. Osial, Overlord of the Vortex, was defeated by Rex Lapis during the Archon War and then summoned by the Fatui Harbinger, Childe, in hopes of luring out Rex Lapis and obtaining his Gnosis for Tsaritsa. Adepti modified the Guizhong Ballista to turn it into an engine of war, and through the joint efforts of the Milleliths, Liyue Qixing, and Adepti, the ancient god was stopped, and Liyue was saved.
After this battle, the Adepti completely entrusted the reign to Liyue Qixing. When Osial's wife, Beisht, wanted to attack Liyue again to avenge her husband, they no longer interfered and allowed the people to defend the city themselves.

customize.text: Eight Adepts

During the Archon War, there was a divine mountain in Liyue with a giant tree on its summit. This tree was a god named "Tao Dou," originally known as "Bune." Back then, people thought that behind Tao Dou was the realm of the dead, and if you committed grave sins in life, your soul would be unable to pass beyond that tree and into the afterlife. About two to three thousand years ago, the Eight Adepts rose up — eight people and beasts who laid down a great magic array to purify Tao Dou. He cared greatly for all living things and volunteered to sanctify himself to pacify the underworld. Without the god's will, not even eight Adepti would have been able to overpower him, much less the Eight Adepts. Tao Dou was sealed in a secret palace in the Qingce Mountains called the "Hidden Palace of Zhou Formula" along with other evil spirits, and the palace itself was enchanted using the Seven-Eight Gates method. After that, Tao Dou's remains sank into the Ley Lines and became a border, separating the living of Liyue from the dead in Liyue. The mortals continued to preserve and maintain the god's new form for thousands of years.

Among the Eight Adepts, there were three joined forces: the Three Hermits of Guizang, the Two Sages of Lianshan, and the Three Beasts of Tao Dou. Although they possessed powers comparable to those of the Adepti, many of them were ordinary mortals. One of the hermits was called "Wind Reader," he came from the Twelve Tribes of the Chenyu Vale, and his descendants became the founders of the Lan clan and the ancient art of Qimen Divination. The second hermit mastered the art of fishing with a rod and line, and became known to the people as the "Yunlai Angler." It is believed that Yunlai Swordsmanship, which Yuheng of the Liyue Qixing, Keqing, uses, was based on Yunlai Angler's rod-wielding techniques. The third hermit was the Wuwang Kid, also known as Old Man Wuwang. According to legend, he always presented himself in child form and was a master of Qihuang sigils, which he used to catch demons, heal disease, and protect lives from the encroaching presence of death. The Lianshan Sages included Sage Hu, a master of gourd crafts, and Sage Jian, an expert in bronze mirrors. Little is known about them, but they were known to have mastered the secret art of Lianshan, earning them the title of the Two Sages of Lianshan. A hidden palace is located deep in the mountains south of the Stone Gate. It is believed to be where they retreated for cultivation. The Three Beasts of Tao Dou, also known as the Three Immortals of Tao Dou, lived on the mountain where the divine tree grew. They were known as the Lone Butterfly of the Crimson Flame, the Jade-Plumed
and the Gold-Eyed Celadon Mare. These were three auspicious beasts, all with the power to take on human form similar to those of the Adepti. During Tao Dou's purification ceremony, the Lone Butterfly sacrificed herself, Silverwing and Wind Reader traveled together, and the white horse went to live in seclusion in the Qingce mountain range. Although they all had remarkable powers, purifying a god of Tao Dou's caliber was no mean feat. They had to use the secret art of Seven-and-Eight-Gates Array, which involved obfuscating one of the gates so that evil couldn't escape. The Lone Butterfly was in charge of the hidden gate that was chosen to be obfuscated, and so she disappeared from the world in the process. According to legend, Old Man Wuwang looked up to her a lot, took up her mantle, and kept her legacy alive, passing it on to the founders of the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor. Thus, the Butterfly sacrificed her life to restore order to the realm of the dead, some chance meetings ensured that future generations continued using her methods to guard the border between life and death. Although she herself disappeared from the world, her mission to protect Liyue is still alive and well, thousands of years on.

customize.text: Celebrations

During the Archon War, the people of Liyue illuminated the night sky with lanterns to serve as a reminder of the way home to their warriors and to never lose sight of themselves. Lantern Rite is an annual festivity to honor these heroes. Fallen Adepti are commemorated during the Lantern Rite in the form of the Mingxiao Lantern — a giant lantern with a Plaustrite as the central stone in them. During the festivals that the Traveler and Paimon attended, Skybracer, Sea Gazer, Menogias, and White Horse Adeptus were commemorated.

In modern Liyue tradition, releasing lanterns with wishes into the sky originates from Lang-Gan. In ancient times, there was a ritual of worshipping Zibai, who showed the people how to use the plow and spade to purge the land of weeds, till the soil, and heap up the earth to make it fertile. Zibai taught the mortals to sow grain and bestowed the promise of life upon every seed. The heavenly messenger blessed the millet and the beans and ensured their stalks and vines stretched forth without end. Zibai graced the wheat and rice so that their heavy heads were filled with plump, glistening grain, and people harvested the fruits of the field, turning them into sacred wine both for honored guests and to present as an offering to the angel. Every step of the ritual had to be performed so that Zibai would witness the depth of the people’s piety and respect. Since the angel was in the sky, people sent their wishes heavenward in the form of lanterns, praying for good fortune and blessings in the coming years.

For many centuries, Liyue has celebrated the Moonchase festival in honor of the Stove God, Marchosius, a dear friend of Rex Lapis who sacrificed his intelligence and power to save Liyue, eventually becoming Guoba. Legend has it that while some Adepti were pursuing the Adeptal path, they would wander across mountains and rivers, enjoying various gourmet dishes, using such means to quiet their hearts. Their path would be called the "Trail of Delicacies" by those who came after. Moonchase originally served as a rite exclusive to the Adepti, but now Moonchase Festival is a celebration of the arrival of the fall by moonlight, when people eat their favorite foods, spend time with friends and relatives, and enjoy the moon and the flowers. The Moonchase Festival has undergone a long evolution, the earliest form being an Adeptal ritual for communicating with the moon known as the "Moonchase Rite." Rex Lapis once personally performed this ceremony in hopes of contacting a fragment of the soul of the
whose soul was sealed in the moon, and after all these years, the moon didn't respond.

customize.text: Legends

There are many legends about Adepti. The first legend is about stone statues that appear all across the vast land of Liyue. Legend has it that in some corners of the land, ancient stone beasts wake at night in the cool of the fall and look around at a world that has slowly become alien to them. Hearing the sounds of frogs and insects greeting them, they respond with deep, soulful cries from their petrified throats. Then they roam around Liyue, inspecting once more the land they used to protect. The elders of Qingce Village say that these statues are illuminated beasts who once fought alongside Rex Lapis in the Archon War. After the war ended, the tide subsided, and peace was restored. The illuminated beasts were no longer required to serve as defenders of the common people, and one by one they retreated to more secluded parts of the country. There they lived free from concern for mortal affairs. But some illuminated beasts remembered with fondness the glorious days when they served under Rex Lapis, and they pined for the years they protected Liyue. Though they were not of the mortal realm, nor were they immortal, for them, too, life would one day come to an end. Thus, they beseeched Rex Lapis to turn their ephemeral flesh bodies into everlasting stone. The merciful Geo Archon granted their request and made them as such.
The second legend tells a story about Qilin, a type of noble, gentle, and benevolent illuminated beast. Qilin often roam the mountain forests but appear only on nights when starlight shines upon clear dew. For sustenance, they drink only spring water and eat only fragrant herbs. It is said that Qilin will never harm living things, refusing even to step on an insect or break a blade of grass. People believe that a Qilin's characteristics, behavior, and every movement are dictated by an age-old etiquette that has remained unchanged for a thousand years. Legend has it that several thousand years ago, a herb gatherer was bathing in a mountain pool when to his surprise, a passing Qilin began to eat the clothes that he had left by the water's edge. The illuminated beast was too young to understand human notions of shame and privacy and had yet to learn the conduct of illuminated beasts in the mortal realm. To make up for her crude behavior and to avoid startling the vulnerable mortal with her otherworldly Adeptal appearance, she transformed into one of human bearing. As the pale light of the full moon fell onto the pool, she appeared before the herb gatherer. Together, they started a journey among flowers and bamboo groves. Qilin interpreted for the mortal the language of the birds, revealed to him the mountain dwelling of the Adepti, and they shared dreams. As the herb gatherer began to stir at the first light of dawn, he awoke to find that the noble illuminated beast had vanished without a trace. Some people say that the Qilin lived together with the mortals, gave birth to children, and grew accustomed to human life.

The third legend is about a martial nomad, Guhua. He was the master of the Rainslasher, a dimly fluorescent greatsword with no sharp edge. Years ago, it was known as the "Beacon of the Nether" by the mountain bandits, because seeing it meant there was no way back. Legend has it that Guhua was an Adeptus. While he lived, bandits dared not act, and the wilderness knew a peace like that of the city. At the end of his journey, Guhua ascended to the heavens in a purple haze and became a star. One to whom Guhua had shown kindness founded what is now known as the Guhua School in his honor. Once, the Guhua Clan was well-known, but now it's a dying art that has been in constant decline for several hundred years.

The fourth legend is a local legend in Fontaine. Many generations ago, a traveler from Fontaine, wandering through Liyue, slipped and fell into a lake. As he sank and gasped for breath, he heard a wondrous tune in the air. They say it was the most beautiful, moving melody he had ever heard. Even in that life-and-death moment, the ethereal music seized his full attention and almost made him forget the fact that he was drowning. When he finally came to, he found that he had already been brought ashore. Not too far from him stood an unfamiliar woman with an almost divine aura. Once she saw that he was no longer in danger, she left without a word. The traveler tried to run after her to show his gratitude. Although a mere dozen paces separated them, no matter how quickly he gave chase, he drew no closer and remained a dozen paces behind. In the end, all he could do was bow in thanks to the woman as he watched her walk away towards the rivers and mountains in the distance before he turned around and made his way home. Once he returned to Fontaine, he began to learn an instrument to spread his story far and wide, just like the bards. After generations of retelling, embellishing, and dramatizing, people have come to think of that lady as something like a fairy. The story's become something of a local legend in Fontaine. It's called "The Lady Overlooking the Lake." People now say that if you go down to the lakeside and play an instrument, so long as you play a pleasing melody, you will hear a fairy lady, who is hiding out of sight, playing along with you.
The fifth legend is about a complex, famous dish in Liyue cuisine, Adeptus' Temptation. Specially selected ingredients are submerged and slowly boiled into soup stock. It is believed that the recipe scribbled from memory alone was enough to urge the Adepti to once again return to the world of men.

The sixth legend tells of the Archon War and Cloud Retainer. In the distant past, before the prosperous port city was ever established, the lords once worshipped as gods fought for reasons of their own. In this fight, the entire mortal world was stained with fire, blood, separation, and betrayal. Those who lost everything in the tumult fled to the mountains, where they begged the Adepti for shelter. Survivors were pursued by countless monsters who had long since lost their senses. Their names were unknown, their forces innumerable. These forces came on like a flood, destroying all in their path. The master the monsters had once revered had fallen. In truth, the fierce roaring of these senseless beasts existed as a final mourning howl. Few mortals were aware that the lord who had once safeguarded these mountains and waters had perished, leaving only a handful of vigilant Yaksha to stand between them and impending disaster. After several days of battle, the monsters came on as an endless horde. According to one version of the legend, when everything hung in the balance, an Adeptus with azure and white feathers burst from the clouds like a descending gale. This Crane-Adeptus turned the tides of a hopeless cause, defeating the flow of monsters. Another version states at this most perilous moment, two jade-carved cranes hurtled from the skies above, unleashing the power of a hail of sigils on the monsters to destroy them as swiftly as a chill wind disperses an expanse of cloud. When the survivors had finally gathered the courage to turn and look, they saw not cranes but a hovering Adeptus with a folding fan in hand. According to a third version, the might of this Adeptus so exceeded mortal capability that the ancestors had heard only the cry of a crane, and before them in an instant, the endless monsters turned to ash like dust as it dissipated into sunlight.

Another legend of the Archon War tells of the Adeptus Skybracer. During the Archon War, there was an epic battle between demons and Adepti. Legend has it that the skies turned black and that winds and waves howled as high as houses. A vile demon struck with all its might, but Skybracer dodged the attack, and the hit landed on Mt. Tianheng with an impact so powerful the base of the mountain cracked. Suddenly, there was a thunderous sound of giant rocks cascading down the mountains, and the whole of Mt. Tianheng was on the verge of collapse. Skybracer knew he had to act quickly, so he summoned a fellow Adeptus, and with the strike of his polearm, this Adeptus tore clean the antlers of the Skybracer's head. Skybracer used his own blood-drenched antlers as a wedge to prop up the mountain. Blood coated his head, and grotesquely, he wiped his hand across his soaked skull, beginning the race back up the mountain to erase the vile demon from the face of the earth. He looked like a king of the demons himself in this moment, but to the sight of the people who lived below the mountain, Skybracer was their savior, a great and merciful Adeptus who had kept them all from certain doom. In this battle, the people thought almost as highly of him as they thought of the Lord of Geo. He fought with the demons until his blood was drained and his life ran out. The blood he lost in the battle turned into the Bishui River, and Mt. Tianheng stands tall and proud to this day because of Skybracer's sacrifice.

Many legends of Liyue make mention of a mysterious White Horse Adeptus. Traces of her tale are found across various books and folktales, with differing accounts of her appearance provided by different sources. The elders of Qingce Village say she became a steed as white as snow and that in the days of the Archon War, she aided Rex Lapis in attaining supremacy over the mortal realm. In the Chenyu Vale, she is considered the "Daughter of Time." Some believe her to be the Gold-Eyed Celadon Mare from The Sanctification of Tao Dou. Others whisper that her eyes, being like amber touched with gold, hold the power to gaze through the desolate wastelands of time itself. And the last insists that she has always lived on the moon, listening to the wishes of mortals while keeping watch over the world of flickering lights below. Although people call her an Adeptus, she did not receive this title from the Prime of Adepti, Morax, having instead been named so by the people. One of the legends about the White Horse Adeptus tells of an encounter with a boy who got lost in a bamboo forest. There, he met a slender woman garbed in white who offered to help drive him out of the forest. While they were spending the night in the woods, she told different stories about three Moons and the times before Archons were born.

<color=#ffffff>"Long ago, three bright moons once hung high in the night sky. These three moons were sisters, their years numbering more than those of the Geo Archon and their year of birth predating the very bedrock upon which Liyue Harbor now rests.</color>
<color=#ffffff>The moons were daughters of prose and song, sovereign over the night sky. They navigated the heavens above in their silver carriage, alternating with one another thrice a month. If the reign was not promptly passed from one sister to the next, a terrible disaster would occur that very day.</color>
<color=#ffffff>These three luminous moons shared but one love, the stars of daybreak. Only at the fleeting moments when day and night converged could one of the three sisters pass the fading stars and gaze upon the chambers of the morning stars. Moments later, as the new dawn would break over the horizon, the carriage would quickly ferry the night's sister away.</color>
<color=#ffffff>The three sisters shared an equal affection for their one and only love, much like the affection they shared for one another. But this was all before the world was smashed against the tides of great calamity.</color>
<color=#ffffff>With time, disasters overturned the sovereign carriage and laid ruin to the halls of the stars. The three sisters of the night turned against one another, leading to their eternal parting by death. Only one of their pale corpses now remains, ever shedding its cold light..."</color>

At dawn, they went their separate ways. In the dawn's glow, the boy heard a whinnying cry that then grew distant. He turned and looked, and there was nothing behind him but a single strand of hair that had come to rest on his shoulder. Many years later, the boy, who was a boy no longer, would remember that moment, and he would understand: the gap between them was like a yawning chasm. His fate was to leave his home and go to Liyue Harbor, to seek the riches the Geo Archon had bestowed upon him. Hers, then, was to hide herself away, away from the majestic, kindly gaze of that great Lord of Geo, and protect those ancient tales that even she was beginning to forget.

A second legend tells of a young man cultivating his arts in the Valley of Hidden Jade who unexpectedly encountered an Adeptus one night as she passed through the same woods. Her stories of distant times enchanted him so much he forgot the moon's rising and falling, the cycle and orbit of stars, and the first croaks of frogs and cries of the cicadas at dawn. The woman in white robes took him on a tour of secluded abodes where the Adepti dwelled and there had him watch an unfinished game of chess and venture to the bottom of a clear river to explore the courts of deceased deities. In their time together, they wandered atop steep cliffs overlooking desolate cities left behind by the mountain tribes. The Adeptus and the young man explored dreams of the fish that played beneath the springs, danced together like ancestral mages revering the serpent, accompanied the demons and gods of the mountain, and fell into deep slumber only when the cicadas had fallen silent. The young man wondered what an Adeptus would think of such a lovely night. Noticing this, she replied to him with a smile, her eyes squinted into slits. She decided to satisfy his curiosity.

The Adepti experienced time differently than mortals. In the eyes of the Adeptus, time was a barren wasteland with neither beginning nor end, blanketed in spider-silk threads stretched to unknown distances. Everything walks or runs — even mountains motionless to mortal sight, may dissipate like rolling clouds here. In her eyes, she sprinted forever alongside all movements, shattering every wave, dispersing all sediment, caring only to run from this moment to the future. The mountain people had viewed her as time's daughter, a white horse leaping from a pure spring, one whom no shackles could bind. The shepherds of the plains had pursued her steps, freeing themselves from the fetters of the wilderness and embarking on a migratory search for the waterweeds, and thus did the golden-white foal blaze the trail for all herds in the land. The kingdom of the ocean depths once saw her as an emissary, their imagination granted her scales and tail plumage, and they fell down to worship her light. In the days when mortals received the blessings of the heavens, great heroes and wandering champions would visit the clear springs in search of her blessing, fighting over the tenderness she left in her hurried wake. When the moon palace collapsed, the chariot fell, and the three moon sisters were slain, these legends were lost along the descent of disaster and downfall of bygone mortals. Trapped within her shell of starry sky, the Adeptus was forced to tarry within the stagnant, foreign land, awaiting her mother's thousand threads and the erosion of hardy stone. When the golden-eyed woman finished her story, the young man had asked her name, to which she had only responded with laughter. Many years later the young man, now old and grey, recalled this moment by chance. By then, he had honed his swordplay to flow like water, founded his own sect, and become a teacher — yet he never could comprehend the final story she told him. As for her, she still sprints along the threads of fate, concealing her trail beneath the forests and springs, far from the gaze of the gods, guarding the ancient stories that slip away, even from her to this day.

According to another legend, the White Horse Adeptus encountered a girl in the forest who had slipped on a cliff and fell as she was gathering herbs for Mora to help her ailing mother. Ziqiao threw the herbs to the fish and offered to tell the girl a story, suggesting that in exchange, she could go on to sell the tale at a bookstore. The Adeptus told her how long ago, when the three moons still shone in the sky, the kingdom of Lang-Gan flourished under their light. This kingdom was the home of the divine
who blessed the lands with gentle winds and generous rain. In gratitude, the people revered her as a Goddess of Soil and Grain. When the moons crumbled and the kingdom lay in ruins, the divine emissary could not accept this fate and granted the people protection. She led the survivors to the east, where they found a new home, and for disobeying the will of the heavens, the divine messenger was imprisoned in the skies, never to see the human world again. After finishing her story, the White Horse Adeptus stated that she had made it up, that it was time for the girl to go home. Suddenly, a wind blew through the forest, and the Adeptus disappeared. Surprised, the girl took off running, and as she left the forest, her ruined home appeared before her, looking as though hundreds of years had passed. Afterwards, the girl awoke where she had fallen, her basket filled with the herbs she had gathered. Just when she grew convinced the incident had been a dream, a white horse galloped over the cliff. As the girl grew up, she told her story to the descendants of the Lu family, the same family who later opened the Baiju Guesthouse in honor of the White Horse Adeptus.

In ancient times, people believed that lunar eclipses were manifestations of the Zhanzhu — toad-like creatures dwelling in the heavens. Each one was plump and bloated like a warty, overfed toad, the Zhanzhu possessed a strange magic that allowed them to steal people's wishes, to suckle upon even the essence of the moon itself. It was believed that on Lantern Rite, when the lanterns first glowed and the full moon shone its brightest, the world was awash in silver light. To the eyes of the Zhanzhu, the full moon is nothing more than a giant, round pancake, waiting to be gnawed and misused for their mischief. Legend has it that one day the Zhanzhu, the Moon Devourer, opened his blood-red maw and let out a long howl, swallowing the full moon in one gulp. Legend has it that like a rice ball, it vanished into his stomach, and at that moment, the world was plunged into darkness, with the little Zhanzhu moving at their master's command, rushing forth to wreak havoc. Suddenly, the White Horse Adeptus appeared, having lived on the moon and being older than the Geo Archon himself. Deprived of moonlight, she found herself surrounded by countless demons. When defeat seemed inevitable, the legend says the villagers of Chenyu Vale released the festival's Xiao Lanterns into the sky, lighting the heavens to aid the Adeptus in battle.
